create-index-lock.title: CREATE INDEX blocks writes
create-index-lock.alt: A recorded run on PostgreSQL. Session A creates an index inside a transaction. Session B's reads still work, but its insert waits until session A commits, because CREATE INDEX holds a lock that conflicts with writes.

steps.note: The transaction holds the index build open, so the lock is easy to see. A real build on a big table holds it for as long as the build takes.
Session A builds an index, which takes a SHARE lock on the table.
Reads are fine: a SHARE lock doesn't conflict with them.
A write isn't. The application's insert now hangs.
Only when the build ends does the insert go through. On a table with hundreds of millions of rows, that could be hours.

create-index-concurrently.title: CONCURRENTLY doesn't block, but it does wait
create-index-concurrently.alt: A recorded run on PostgreSQL. Session A has a transaction open. Session B starts CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which waits for that older transaction to finish. Meanwhile a third session's inserts go through without waiting. When session A commits, the index build completes.

steps.note: Session A opens a transaction and does some work.

steps.sql: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_total ON orders (total)
steps.note: The concurrent build can't finish while an older transaction might still change the table, so it waits.
But it blocks nobody. A new insert goes straight through.
Session A finishes. Now the build can complete, and the statement returns.

plan-cost.title: What the planner expects each plan to cost
plan-cost.alt: The planner's estimated cost of three plans for one query as the share of matching rows grows from 0.001% to 100% of a million-row table. Index Scan is cheapest for very few rows, Bitmap Heap Scan takes over in the middle, and Seq Scan is flat and becomes cheapest once a large share matches.

plan-time.title: What each plan really took, from a warm cache
plan-time.alt: Measured time of the same three plans on the same query from a warm cache. The lines cross at different places from the planner's estimates, because the planner's default costs assume random page reads are four times as slow as sequential ones.

plans.title: Watch the plan change
plans.hint: 100,000 rows with an index on x. Each preset asks for a different share of the table. Read the top line of each plan.
plans.query:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT name FROM t WHERE x = 500;

presets.label: 1 row: index scan
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT name FROM t WHERE id = 500;

presets.label: 2% of rows: bitmap
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT name FROM t WHERE x < 2000;

presets.label: 50% of rows: seq scan
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT name FROM t WHERE x < 50000;

presets.label: Index only
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT x FROM t WHERE x < 500;

presets.label: Function on the column
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT name FROM t WHERE x + 1 = 501;

composite.title: The leftmost column rule
composite.hint: A composite index on (a, b). Which of these can use it? Edit the WHERE clause, or create another index and run them again.
